headline: Cape May Rips picky, Bay weakfish building — drum's long gone
subhead: August sun has the rips running slow and choosy while Delaware Bay's weakfish grounds keep filling in on schedule.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

Rips: fishable, not fast. Hereford Inlet: bluefish on the move. Delaware Bay: weakfish building like it should. Drum: done, don't bother. That's the report card for the first week of August, and there's no dressing it up beyond that.

The Cape May Rips in high summer are what they are — thin current on the small tides, warm surface water stacked on top of cooler bottom water, and stripers that know exactly where the bait is concentrated and won't chase much outside of it. Boats working the ledges off Cape May Point in 30 to 40 feet are finding keepers mixed with a lot of short fish on the last two hours of the ebb sliding into the top of the flood — that's when the rip lines actually stand up enough to hold bait against the structure. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom through the seams, are outproducing anything worked fast or up in the water column. If you're marking bait high and the current's weak, don't waste time up top — the fish are down on the structure waiting for it to funnel to them. This time of year the rips reward patience over hardware. Run three or four drifts through a piece before you decide it's dead.

Bluefish are the more reliable player right now. Bunker pods have been pushing through the surf zone off the Point and inside Hereford Inlet, and when those pods bunch up tight against the beach or a current seam, the blues turn it into a genuine topwater event — poppers, Hopkins jigs, anything chrome and loud will draw a strike. It's not subtle fishing and it doesn't need to be. Chopper blues in the 4 to 8-pound class have been common in those blitzes, and if you find the bait balled up tight, don't leave it — that window can shut as fast as it opens once the pod scatters or moves offshore.

Fluke fishing in the back bay channels has stayed the most dependable piece of the puzzle. Kimbles, the Cape May Canal drop-offs, and the deeper bends off the ICW have been giving up keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range on white or chartreuse Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing when the water's clean and moving. Bounce bottom, keep contact, and don't overwork the retrieve — fluke in August want it presented slow and steady more than jigged hard.

Weakfish are the story worth paying attention to. We flagged this a couple weeks back — said the numbers would keep building into a real pattern instead of a one-week flash, and that's exactly the shape it's taking on the Bay reef sites. Ship John Shoal and the rubble around Miah Maull have been holding weakfish in respectable numbers on the dropping tide, with the better fish coming after dark on shad-tipped bucktails and squid strips fished slow along the bottom edges of the reef structure. It's not a blitz-style bite — it's a working man's bite, methodical drifts through the same stretch of structure until you find where they're stacked that evening. Worth noting: these fish move on the tide, not the clock, so if the first drift doesn't produce, shift with the current rather than anchoring up and waiting.

And the black drum — if you're still thinking about that, stop. The Bay's drum run is a May event, and by August those fish have long since pushed out and dispersed. Nothing productive happening there now, and anyone telling you otherwise on the Bay side is selling a memory, not a report.

Triggerfish have been showing around the rock piles at the Hereford Inlet jetties and the rubble sections of the Cape May Canal, which is normal for this time of year once the water holds steady in the mid-70s. Small fish mostly, biting on clam and crab baits fished tight to structure on light tackle — a fun sideshow if you're bottom fishing that zone and want variety, not a target species worth building a whole trip around yet.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if the heat and the light southwest breeze stick around — the rips stay picky but fishable on the tide windows, the bluefish keep working the bunker as long as those pods stay thick along the beach, and the weakfish should keep filling in on the reef sites through the rest of August. If a cooler front pushes through and knocks the surface temps down even a couple degrees, that's when I'd expect the rips to wake up with better current and less lockjaw on the bigger bass. Until then, fish the tide windows tight, don't burn gas chasing sonar returns that aren't holding still, and treat the weakfish grounds as the most consistent bet on the schedule right now.
